title: Build Your Own Container
text:
NoteBy the end of this guide, you should be able to…




Set up a Linux environment to build containers on a Mac, Windows, or Linux machine, and choose the right one for your situation
Read an Apptainer definition file (.def) section by section and explain what each part does
Build a container image from a definition file with apptainer build
Explain what a container registry is, why images are versioned, and what your options are for sharing one — well enough to research the specifics
Recognize the risk of a published image drifting from its definition, and the manual and automated ways to prevent it
Adapt the whole pattern to your own analysis
In the workshop you used and modified a pre-built container. This guide is about authoring one. It’s self-paced — work through it at your own speed, and come back to it when you’re ready to containerize your own research.

title: Build Your Own Container
text:
Step 0 — Get a Linux environment
You have four honest options, from least to most commitment. Pick based on how often you’ll do this and how much you want a persistent local setup.









Option
Best for
Install cost
Persists?




GitHub Codespaces
Trying this out; occasional builds
None (browser)
No — ephemeral


Lima (macOS)
Mac users who build regularly
Moderate
Yes


WSL2 (Windows)
Windows users who build regularly
Moderate
Yes


Native Linux
You already run Linux
None
Yes




Option A — GitHub Codespaces (easiest start)
This is the same environment you used in the workshop, and it can build images too, not just run them. Open a Codespace on a repo whose .devcontainer is privileged (the workshop repo already is — see the note below), then jump to Step 1.






TipWhy the Codespace must be “privileged”





Apptainer creates Linux user namespaces to run and build containers. A Codespace is itself a container, and nested user namespaces are blocked unless the container runs privileged. The workshop repo’s .devcontainer/devcontainer.json sets "runArgs": ["--privileged"] for exactly this reason. If you build your own Codespace config, you need that line or apptainer will fail with “Failed to create user namespace.”



Tradeoff: zero install, but the environment is ephemeral — anything not committed or pushed disappears when the Codespace is deleted.


Option B — Lima (macOS)
Lima runs a real Linux VM on your Mac. Because it’s a genuine VM (not a nested container), user namespaces work natively — no privileged tricks needed.
brew install lima
limactl start                 # launches an Ubuntu VM (accept the defaults)
limactl shell default         # drop into the Linux VM
# ...now you're on Linux. Install Apptainer (Step 1) inside here.
Tradeoff: a few GB of disk and a VM to maintain, but a fast, persistent local Linux you fully control.


Option C — WSL2 (Windows)
WSL2 gives Windows a real Linux kernel. User namespaces work, so Apptainer runs normally.
wsl --install -d Ubuntu       # in PowerShell; reboot if prompted
Then open the Ubuntu terminal and continue with Step 1 inside it.
Tradeoff: moderate one-time setup, then a persistent Ubuntu integrated with Windows.


Option D — Native Linux
Nothing to set up — go straight to Step 1.


Install Apptainer (all options except Codespaces, which has it already)
# Debian/Ubuntu (Lima, WSL2, or native Ubuntu)
APPTAINER_VERSION=1.3.6
cd /tmp
wget https://github.com/apptainer/apptainer/releases/download/v${APPTAINER_VERSION}/apptainer_${APPTAINER_VERSION}_amd64.deb
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y ./apptainer_${APPTAINER_VERSION}_amd64.deb
apptainer --version






Note



We pin a specific version (1.3.6) on purpose — pinning is the same reproducibility habit you’ll apply to the image itself below. The non-suid package shown here runs rootless via user namespaces, which is what you want on a personal machine.

title: Build Your Own Container
section: Step 1 — Read the definition file, line by line
text:
Step 1 — Read the definition file, line by line
A definition file is the recipe for your environment. Here is the workshop’s _materials/container/deseq2.def, with every section explained.
Bootstrap: docker
From: bioconductor/bioconductor_docker:RELEASE_3_23-R-4.6.1
Bootstrap / From — where the build starts. Bootstrap: docker means “pull a starting image from a Docker/OCI registry.” From: names that image.
Why bioconductor/bioconductor_docker:RELEASE_3_23-R-4.6.1? Because it already contains R, BiocManager, and — crucially — the system libraries needed to compile Bioconductor packages. Starting from a bare Ubuntu would mean installing all of that by hand. Why the RELEASE_3_23-R-4.6.1 tag? A Bioconductor release pins a specific R version and a specific set of package versions. Pinning the tag is what makes the build reproducible: :latest would silently change underneath you.
Note the tag names the R patch version too. A bare RELEASE_3_23 would fix the Bioconductor release but let R move if the image were rebuilt — the same silent drift, one level down. Pin as much as the registry lets you.
%labels
    Author       ARCS Workshop ...
    Description  DESeq2 ...
    Version      1.0
%labels — metadata baked into the image. Readable later with apptainer inspect deseq2.sif. Good place to record a version.
%help
    Reproducible R environment for the ARCS Part 4 DESeq2 pipeline...
%help — free text shown by apptainer run-help deseq2.sif. Document how to run the image so the next person (often future-you) doesn’t have to guess.
%post
    R -e 'BiocManager::install(c("DESeq2"), update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)'
    R -e 'install.packages(c("ggplot2"), repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")'
    R -e 'library(DESeq2); library(ggplot2)'
%post — commands run once, at build time, inside the image. This is where you install everything your analysis needs. It’s the slow step (Bioconductor compiles), which is exactly why you build once and reuse the result. Note the two package worlds: Bioconductor packages go through BiocManager::install(); CRAN packages through install.packages(). The final library(...) line makes the build fail loudly if anything didn’t install, rather than shipping a broken image.
%environment
    export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
    export LANG=C.UTF-8
%environment — variables set every time the container runs (not at build time). Locale settings here keep R’s text handling consistent across hosts.
%runscript
    exec Rscript scripts/pipeline.R "$@"
%runscript — the default action of apptainer run deseq2.sif. Here it runs the pipeline in the current directory. (apptainer exec ... Rscript scripts/pipeline.R does the same thing explicitly; run just bakes in the default.)
%test
    R -e 'stopifnot(requireNamespace("DESeq2", quietly = TRUE)); cat("DESeq2 OK\n")'
%test — runs automatically at the end of the build to sanity-check the image. If DESeq2 didn’t install, the build fails here instead of in front of your collaborators.

title: Build Your Own Container
text:
Step 2 — Build the image
From the folder containing the .def file:
cd workshops/arcs_04/_materials/container
apptainer build deseq2.sif deseq2.def






WarningThis is slow — that’s normal



Building this image compiles DESeq2 and its dependencies. Expect several minutes to ~20+ minutes depending on your machine and network. You’ll see pages of compiler output scroll by. That long compile is precisely why we never build live in class and instead distribute the finished .sif.


When it finishes you’ll see your %test print DESeq2 OK and a deseq2.sif file appear. Common hiccups:

Out of disk space — the build cache plus the base image can need several GB. Free space, or run apptainer cache clean.
Network flake during package install — re-run the build; it’s the %post downloads failing, not your .def.
“Failed to create user namespace” — you’re in a nested container that isn’t privileged (see Step 0).

title: Build Your Own Container
text:
Step 3 — Test it locally
Before publishing, confirm the image actually runs your analysis:
cd ..                                   # back to _materials/
apptainer exec container/deseq2.sif R --version
apptainer exec container/deseq2.sif Rscript scripts/pipeline.R
ls outputs/tables/ outputs/figures/
If outputs/ fills with results, your image is good to ship.

section: Step 4 — Sharing your image: the concept
text:
Step 4 — Sharing your image: the concept
Steps 0–3 are the part you can do today. What follows is a concept orientation, not a walkthrough — enough vocabulary to know what exists and what to search for when you need it.
Once you have a working .sif, the question becomes: how does anyone else get it? Image files are large — often several gigabytes — so they don’t belong in a Git repository. They live somewhere else, and your repo points at them.
A registry is a server that stores and serves container images, the way CRAN serves R packages. You upload (“push”) an image once; collaborators, an HPC cluster, or an automated job download (“pull”) it by name. The common choices are the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), which sits next to your code, Docker Hub, Quay.io, and the Apptainer-native Sylabs Cloud Library. Pushing requires an account and an access token with permission to write packages; images are private by default, so there’s a visibility setting to flip if you want people to pull without logging in.






ImportantYou’d publish to your namespace, not ours



The workshop image lives at ghcr.io/cwml/cwml_arcs_4_deseq2 — you can pull from it, but you can’t push to it. Publishing means creating your own registry namespace under your GitHub account or your lab’s organization. That’s an account setup task, not a container task, which is why it isn’t a step you can follow along with here.


Version tags are the idea worth carrying away even if you never push anything. A registry name ends in a tag — :1.0, :latest. Give an image a real version and bump it whenever the .def changes, rather than overwriting :latest forever. The payoff: a methods section can cite the exact environment a result came from, and a colleague asking for that version gets precisely what you ran. Treat the image tag as a Git tag for your environment.
Two lighter-weight alternatives are worth knowing about. You can attach a .sif to a GitHub Release — no registry account, works well for a single occasional artifact. Or deposit the image in Zenodo, which mints a DOI you can cite in a paper and guarantees long-term archival. For published research, the Zenodo route is often the more appropriate one.






TipWhat to search for






apptainer push, apptainer pull, apptainer registry login — the three commands involved
ORAS — the protocol Apptainer uses to store .sif files in OCI registries; you’ll see oras:// prefixes in registry addresses
GHCR authentication, personal access token, write:packages scope, package visibility — the GitHub account-side setup
Sylabs Cloud Library — the registry built specifically for Apptainer/Singularity
Zenodo DOI software archiving — for citable, permanent deposits

title: Build Your Own Container
section: Step 5 — Keeping the image in sync: the concept
text:
Step 5 — Keeping the image in sync: the concept
Here’s the failure mode that eventually bites everyone: you edit the .def, commit it, and forget to rebuild. Now the recipe in your repo and the published image describe different environments — and there’s nothing to warn you. The image people are actually using no longer matches the definition people are actually reading. That’s a reproducibility bug that looks like nothing at all.
The low-tech answer is discipline, and it’s genuinely sufficient for most projects: whenever you change the .def, rebuild, bump the version tag, and note the current image version in your README. Because the change is a Git commit, you have a record of when the environment changed and why.
The automated answer is continuous integration (CI) — a service that watches your repository and runs jobs when something changes. Configured for this purpose, it rebuilds and republishes the image automatically whenever the .def file is modified, so the published image cannot drift from the definition. On GitHub this is GitHub Actions: a YAML file in .github/workflows/ describing what to run and what should trigger it. Notably, CI runners are full virtual machines rather than nested containers, so the privileged-mode problem from Step 0 doesn’t arise there.






NoteThis one is genuinely a later topic



CI is a substantial subject of its own — worth learning, but not a prerequisite for containerizing your research. Manual rebuilds with honest version tags get you the reproducibility benefit. Come back to automation when rebuilding by hand starts to feel like the thing you keep forgetting.
This repository does have such a workflow, at .github/workflows/build-image.yml, if you want to see a real one.








TipWhat to search for






GitHub Actions workflow syntax — the structure of the YAML file
workflow triggers, path filters — running a job only when specific files change
setup-apptainer GitHub Action — installs Apptainer on a runner
GITHUB_TOKEN, workflow permissions — how a job authenticates to push a package without a personal token
continuous integration generally — the concept is not container-specific

section: Step 6 — Adapt the pattern to your own analysis
text:
Step 6 — Adapt the pattern to your own analysis
This is the real goal. To containerize your work, repeat the same moves:

List your dependencies. What language/version, and which packages? For R, skim your library() / pacman::p_load() calls. Split them into CRAN vs. Bioconductor (or pip vs. conda for Python).
Pick a base image. Match the heavy lifting to your stack: a Bioconductor image for Bioc work, rocker/r-ver:4.4.1 for plain R, python:3.12-slim for Python. Pin the tag.
Write the .def. Copy deseq2.def and edit the %post installs. Keep the %runscript pointing at your entry script and the %test checking your key package loads.
Build and test (Steps 2–3) until your pipeline runs inside the image.
Share it when you need to (Steps 4–5). A local .sif plus a committed .def is already reproducible for you and anyone who can rebuild. Reach for a registry when collaborators, a cluster, or a publication need the exact image.







Tip



Keep the .def, your pipeline script, and a small example dataset together in the repo — exactly like _materials/. That folder is your reproducible project: someone can clone it, pull the image, and reproduce your results on any Linux host, including HPC.

title: Build Your Own Container
text:
Recap

Building needs Linux — Codespaces to start, Lima/WSL2 for a persistent local setup.
The .def file is a readable recipe; each section has one job.
apptainer build turns the recipe into a single .sif image (slow, once).
Images are too large for Git — a registry, a GitHub Release, or a Zenodo deposit is how one gets shared. A real version tag is what makes it citable.
A published image can silently drift from its definition. Rebuild and bump the version whenever the .def changes; automate it with CI later.
The same pattern containerizes any analysis — which is the whole point of the ARCS series.

Where we are in the series

text:
Today’s workflow
Six steps, in order:

Launch a Codespace — everyone gets an identical Linux machine
Verify that Apptainer and the pre-built image are in place
Run the DESeq2 pipeline from the container
Read the definition file that built the image
Modify a parameter, re-run, and watch the result change
Connect it all back to Git

We use a pre-built image rather than building one from scratch — building compiles Bioconductor and takes far longer than a session allows. Authoring your own image is the self-paced follow-up guide.

title: Apptainer
text:
Why containers?
In Parts 1–3 you may have hit a familiar wall: code that runs on one computer fails on another. A package version differs, an operating system handles something differently, a dependency is missing. “It works on my machine” is the opposite of reproducible research.
A container packages your entire computing environment — the R installation, every package at a pinned version, the system libraries underneath — into a single file. Anyone who runs that file gets exactly the environment you built, regardless of what their own computer looks like.
The key word is entire. You may already pin your R packages with something like renv — that’s the same instinct, one layer up. But a package lockfile still assumes R itself is installed, at a compatible version, on an operating system that has the right system libraries for those packages to compile against. A container removes those assumptions by shipping all of it. Think of renv as a shopping list and a container as the delivered groceries.






NoteIs a container a virtual machine?



No — and the difference is why containers are practical.
A virtual machine simulates an entire computer, including its own operating-system kernel. That’s heavy: gigabytes of overhead, slow to start.
A container shares the host’s Linux kernel and packages only the layers above it — the software, libraries, and files. That’s why an image starts in seconds and why apptainer exec feels like running a normal command rather than booting a machine.
It’s also why Apptainer needs Linux specifically: it isn’t simulating a Linux kernel, it’s borrowing the one already running.

title: Apptainer
text:
The words you’ll hear today
Four terms get used constantly and they’re easy to blur together:







Term
What it is




Container
The general idea: software packaged with everything it needs to run


Image (.sif)
The actual file on disk — one self-contained artifact you can copy, share, or archive. .sif stands for Singularity Image Format


Apptainer
The program that runs images (and builds them). It’s what you type at the command line


Definition file (.def)
The plain-text recipe describing what goes into an image. Human-readable, lives in your repo, gets version controlled



The relationship, end to end: you write a definition file, Apptainer builds it into an image, and then Apptainer runs that image to execute your analysis. Today you’ll do only the last part — the image is already built for you.

title: Apptainer
text:
So what is Apptainer?
Apptainer is free, open-source software that builds and runs containers, purpose-built for research computing. You install it on a Linux machine; from then on it’s a command-line program, and the handful of subcommands you’ll meet today (exec, run, pull, build) are most of what anyone uses day to day.
It was created at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to solve a problem research computing had and web infrastructure didn’t: how do you let hundreds of untrusted users run custom software environments on a shared cluster without handing any of them administrator rights? Apptainer’s answer is that a container runs as you — with your permissions, your files, your identity — rather than as a privileged system user. That single design decision is why essentially every academic HPC centre supports it.






TipYou’ll also see the name “Singularity”



Apptainer was called Singularity until 2021, when the project joined the Linux Foundation and was renamed. They are the same tool.
This matters practically: papers, tutorials, and Stack Overflow answers from before ~2022 all say “Singularity,” and many HPC clusters still provide the command as singularity rather than apptainer. If your cluster’s docs mention Singularity, everything you learn here applies — try singularity exec in place of apptainer exec.








NoteWhy Apptainer and not Docker?



You may have heard of Docker. Same core idea, different conventions:

Apptainer is built for research computing and HPC
It runs as you, not as root — which is why shared clusters allow it
An image is one portable file (analysis.sif) you can copy, archive, or publish alongside a paper, rather than a set of layers in a daemon’s storage

Docker is excellent for web services; Apptainer is the norm in research computing because of that security model on shared systems. Apptainer can also read Docker images, which is why our definition file starts from one.








ImportantThe OS limitation is the lesson



Apptainer only runs on Linux. There is no Mac or Windows version.
That sounds like a problem — but it’s actually the whole point. The reason containers exist is that the host operating system should not constrain what runs inside. To use a container you still need a Linux kernel somewhere:

On a Mac or Windows laptop, that “somewhere” is the GitHub Codespace we’re about to open.
On a research cluster, it’s the HPC login node.
On a Linux laptop, it’s just there.

Once you cross into that Linux environment, the container behaves identically everywhere. That’s reproducibility you can hand to a colleague.

title: Apptainer
text:
Host vs. container









Host environment
Container environment




What it is
Whatever R/packages are installed on the machine you’re using
A fixed, pinned environment baked into an image file (.sif)


Who controls it
Each user, differently
Whoever wrote the definition file — once, for everyone


Reproducible?
Only if everyone matches versions by hand
Yes — same image = same environment, every time


When to use it
Quick interactive work, exploration
Sharing an analysis, publishing, running on HPC



In Hour 1 you ran the DESeq2 analysis on your host (Positron on your own laptop). Now you’ll run the same analysis from a container — and get the same answer, on a different operating system.

title: Apptainer
text:
Step 1 — Launch the Codespace
A Codespace is a Linux computer that runs in your browser. Opening one from our workshop repository gives everyone — Mac, Windows, or Linux — the identical environment.

Go to the workshop repository: github.com/CWML/ARCS
Click the green < > Code button → Codespaces tab → Create codespace on main.
Wait for it to build. The first time, it automatically installs Apptainer and downloads our pre-built DESeq2 image — you’ll see progress in the terminal.







Tip



When the terminal shows Setup complete., you’re ready. This takes a couple of minutes the first time; that’s the environment being assembled for you so you don’t have to.








NoteWhat just happened? (the .devcontainer)





The repository contains a .devcontainer/ folder that tells Codespaces how to set itself up. Its setup.sh script installed Apptainer and ran apptainer pull to download our pre-built image to ~/deseq2.sif. You didn’t install anything — the recipe is in the repo, so it’s the same for everyone.

title: Apptainer
text:
Step 2 — Verify the environment
Open the terminal in your Codespace (Ctrl + `) and confirm the pieces are in place:
# Apptainer is installed
apptainer --version

# The pre-built image is present
ls -lh ~/deseq2.sif

# R lives INSIDE the container — ask the container for its R version
apptainer exec ~/deseq2.sif R --version
That last command is the key idea: you don’t have R installed on this Codespace. R lives inside deseq2.sif. apptainer exec <image> <command> runs a command inside the container’s environment.

title: Apptainer
section: Step 3 — Run the DESeq2 pipeline from the container
text:
Step 3 — Run the DESeq2 pipeline from the container
The pipeline code and a subset of the Shank3 dataset live in the repo under workshops/arcs_04/_materials/. Move there and run the pipeline inside the container:
cd workshops/arcs_04/_materials
apptainer exec ~/deseq2.sif Rscript scripts/pipeline.R
Apptainer automatically makes your current folder available inside the container, so the pipeline can read processed_data/ and write outputs/.






NoteWhat’s inside the image, and what isn’t



This is worth being precise about, because it’s the piece most people get backwards at first.
Inside the image: R, DESeq2, ggplot2, and the system libraries they need — the software. Fixed at build time and identical for everyone.
Outside the image: your code (scripts/pipeline.R), your data (processed_data/), and your results (outputs/) — all ordinary files in your own folder, which Apptainer makes visible to the container while it runs.
That’s the division of labour. The environment is frozen and shared; your files stay yours, editable with normal tools. It’s why you can edit scripts/pipeline.R in Step 5 with the plain editor and immediately re-run it — you never have to open up or rebuild the image to change your analysis.


When it finishes you’ll see a summary like:
========================================================
Contrast : genotype  Shank3 vs WT
Design   : ~ genotype   (condition == 'normal' only)
Cutoffs  : padj < 0.05   |log2FC| > 1
Significant genes: <N>  (of <M> tested)
Tables  -> outputs/tables/
Figures -> outputs/figures/
========================================================
Look at what it produced:
ls outputs/tables/ outputs/figures/
outputs/tables/

DESeq2_Shank3vsWT_allGenes.csv — every gene tested, sorted by adjusted p-value
DESeq2_Shank3vsWT_sigDEGs.csv — the differentially expressed genes
normCounts_Shank3vsWT.csv — size-factor-normalized counts

outputs/figures/ — open these from the file explorer

PCA_Shank3vsWT.png — samples in PC space, coloured by genotype
SampleDistances_Shank3vsWT.png — sample-to-sample distance heatmap
MAplot_Shank3vsWT.png, Volcano_Shank3vsWT.png — the results

This is the same outputs/figures/ + outputs/tables/ split Hour 1 uses, so you can compare the two runs file for file.
Each filename also ends in a Run ID — a timestamp like PCA_Shank3vsWT_20260730-144530.png. Re-running never overwrites earlier results, which is what lets you compare runs in Step 5.






Note



This is the same analysis you ran in Hour 1 — but it just ran on Linux, inside a pinned environment, on a machine that isn’t yours, and gave the same result. That’s the payoff.

title: Apptainer
section: Step 4 — Look inside the definition file
text:
Step 4 — Look inside the definition file
The image didn’t appear from nowhere. It was built from a definition file, _materials/container/deseq2.def. Open it. Each section has a job:
Bootstrap: docker
From: bioconductor/bioconductor_docker:RELEASE_3_23-R-4.6.1   # the starting point

%post          # commands run ONCE at build time — installs DESeq2, ggplot2
%environment   # variables set every time the container runs
%runscript     # the default action of `apptainer run`
%test          # a sanity check run at the end of the build
The whole reproducible environment is described by this one readable text file. Because it lives in the repo next to your code, anyone can see — and rebuild — exactly what your analysis ran inside.






TipWhy don’t we rebuild it live?





Building the image compiles DESeq2 and its dependencies, which takes many minutes. So we build it once, ahead of time, and everyone uses the result. Building your own image from scratch is covered in the follow-up self-paced guide.

title: Apptainer
section: Step 5 — Make a change and re-run
text:
Step 5 — Make a change and re-run
Reproducible doesn’t mean frozen — it means controlled. Let’s change the analysis and watch the result change, with the same image.
Open scripts/pipeline.R and find the parameters block at the top:
PADJ      <- 0.05      # adjusted p-value (FDR) cutoff
LFC       <- 1         # |log2 fold change| cutoff
CONDITION <- "normal"  # which condition to keep
Right now a gene must clear both bars: statistically significant and at least a two-fold change (|log2FC| > 1). Drop the effect-size bar and keep every statistically significant gene:
LFC       <- 0
Save, and re-run exactly as before:
apptainer exec ~/deseq2.sif Rscript scripts/pipeline.R
The Significant genes count jumps from 3 to 16. Same environment, same data, same code — you asked a different question and got a different answer. That’s a controlled, reproducible experiment.
Your first run is still there. Every filename carries a Run ID timestamp, so this run sat alongside it rather than overwriting it:
ls outputs/tables/
wc -l outputs/tables/DESeq2_Shank3vsWT_sigDEGs_*.csv
Two tables, both kept — 4 and 17 lines, which is a header row plus 3 genes and a header row plus 16. Being able to put two runs next to each other is what turns a change into evidence rather than just a new number.






NoteWhat you just changed



PADJ is about statistical significance — how confident we are the difference is real. LFC is about biological significance — how large the difference is. Setting LFC <- 0 keeps genes that are reliably different but only slightly so. Neither bar is the “right” one; which you use depends on the question you’re asking.


Now that the effect-size filter is off, PADJ has room to bite too — try PADJ <- 0.01 and re-run for 16 → 9.






Tip



Try another: set CONDITION <- "sleep_deprived" to run the identical Shank3-vs-WT comparison in the other condition, and re-run. Every plot and table regenerates for the new subset.

title: Apptainer
section: Step 6 — It all travels together (back to Git)
text:
Step 6 — It all travels together (back to Git)
Look at what’s in the repository now:

scripts/pipeline.R — the analysis code
container/deseq2.def — the environment definition
processed_data/ — the data
the pre-built image, published to a registry (ghcr.io/cwml/cwml_arcs_4_deseq2)

This is the Part 3 Git story completed. Your code was already version controlled. Now the environment it runs in is captured too — as a text file you can diff, and as a published image anyone can pull. Clone the repo, open a Codespace (or use HPC), apptainer pull, and run. The analysis reproduces. That is the goal of the whole ARCS series, made concrete.

title: Apptainer
text:

title: Git & Version Control
text:
Introduction
In this session we’ll take a project that lives only on your computer and give it a full version history and an online home. We’ll use three tools, each with one clear job:



Tool
Its job




Positron
Build your local commit history


GitHub Desktop
The bridge — publish and sync, no SSH setup


GitHub.com
The remote — host and view your project online



Everything in the first half happens locally on your own computer. In the second half we connect that local project to GitHub.






TipGoing Further



The appendices at the end cover collaboration (fork & Pull Requests), the command-line git workflow, SSH key setup, and Yale’s GitHub Enterprise options. They’re written so you can work through them on your own after the session.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
0. Why Version Control?
You’ve probably seen a folder like this:
analysis.R
analysis_v2.R
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_FINAL.R
analysis_final_FINAL_really.R
This is version control done by hand — and it’s painful. You can’t remember what changed between versions, you can’t safely delete any of them, and collaborating means emailing files back and forth.
Git solves this. It’s a time machine for your project: it saves snapshots (called commits) of your work over time, so you can always see what changed, when, and why — and roll back if you need to. Instead of five copies of a file, you keep one file with a complete history.






NoteGit vs. GitHub




Git is the tool that tracks changes on your computer (local).
GitHub is a website that hosts git projects online (remote), so you can back them up and share them.

You can use git entirely on its own. GitHub adds the online home.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
0.5 Preflight: Is Git Initialized?
Before we use Positron’s Source Control tab, let’s confirm that git is actually tracking your project. When you created your R project you may have checked “Initialize git repository” — but not everyone did, and that’s fine.
Open the Terminal tab in Positron (or use the menu: Terminal → New Terminal). Because you’re working inside an R project, Positron automatically opens the terminal in your project folder — so you don’t need to navigate anywhere first.
git status
You’ll see one of two things:

✅ Git is ready❌ Not a git repository


On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        data/
        scripts/
        ...
Your repository is already initialized. Move on to Section 1.


fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
Run one command to fix it:
git init
You should see:
Initialized empty Git repository in /path/to/your/project/.git/
Now run git status again — you should see the “Git is ready” output above.









TipWhy the terminal?



Positron’s Source Control tab is a visual interface built on top of the same git commands you just ran. Starting here lets you see what’s happening under the hood before we switch to the GUI — and git init is the one thing the GUI can’t do for you.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
1. Local Git in Positron
Your control center for git in Positron is the Source Control tab in the left activity bar (the same panel used in VS Code).
Action: Click the Source Control tab. If there are no pending changes, the panel will be empty — that just means git doesn’t see any unsaved modifications right now.

The Core Workflow: Modify → Stage → Commit
Every change you save to your history goes through three steps:

Modify — you edit files in your project as usual
Stage — you pick which changes to include in the next snapshot
Commit — you save those staged changes as a permanent snapshot

The “stage” step is what surprises newcomers: git lets you choose exactly what goes into each commit, so you can group related changes together instead of dumping everything at once.


Reading the Status Indicators
When you change files, they appear in the Source Control panel with a letter. These are the three you’ll see most often:



Indicator
Meaning




U
Untracked — a new file git doesn’t know about yet


M
Modified — an existing file has changed


A
Added — a new file that’s been staged, ready to commit









TipTwo Zones



The panel has two areas: Changes (modified but not yet staged) and Staged Changes (packed and ready to commit). Clicking the + next to a file moves it from Changes → Staged Changes.




Your First Commit

Look at the Source Control tab. You should see several files listed as untracked (U) — the R scripts and data files you’ve worked with throughout the workshop.
Stage everything. Hover over the Changes heading and click the + icon to stage all files at once. They move down into Staged Changes.
Write a commit message. In the message box at the top of the panel, type something descriptive:
Add workshop scripts and data from Parts 1 and 2
Commit. Click the ✓ Commit button.

Congratulations — that’s your first snapshot of the project!






TipWrite Messages for Your Future Self



A good commit message finishes the sentence “This commit will…”. Add data loading script is useful; stuff and update are not.




A Second Commit
Let’s do the cycle once more with a small change.

Make an edit. Open any R script and add a comment line at the top, for example:

# Analysis script — tracked with git

Check the panel. The file now shows an M (modified) under Changes.
Review the diff (recommended). Click the filename to open a diff view — additions in green, deletions in red. Reviewing the diff before committing is the single best habit for catching mistakes early.
Stage and commit. Click + to stage the file, type Add header comment to analysis script, and click ✓ Commit.

You’ve completed a second version-control cycle.






NoteOptional: A Peek Behind the Curtain



The Source Control panel just runs git commands for you. If you open the Terminal tab and run:
git status
git log --oneline
you’ll see the current state and the list of commits you just made. You never have to use the terminal — but it’s good to know the GUI isn’t doing anything magic. The full command-line workflow is in Appendix B.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
2. Excluding Data Files: The .gitignore File
An important best practice: don’t store large data files in git.
Git is built for code and text, not big datasets:

Repository bloat — git keeps every version of every file, so a 100 MB dataset can balloon your repo after a few edits
GitHub limits — 100 MB per-file limit; repos should stay under 1 GB
Wrong tool for the job — git compresses text well but handles large binary data poorly







NoteWhere Should Data Live Instead?










Data Size
Recommended Approach




Small reference data (< 10 MB)
OK to include if it rarely changes


Medium (10 MB–1 GB)
Cloud storage (Dropbox, Drive, OneDrive) — document the location


Large (> 1 GB)
Institutional repositories, OSF, Zenodo, Figshare


Very large
Git LFS — stores big files externally, keeps references in git






Extend the Existing .gitignore File
You already have a .gitignore in your project root — renv::init() created it back in Part 1 to exclude its package cache. We just need to open it and add rules for our data folders.

Open it. In Positron’s Explorer pane, click .gitignore in your project root. (If you don’t see it, make sure hidden files are visible: toggle with View → Show Hidden Files.)
Add these lines below what’s already there:

# Ignore data folders
raw_data/
processed_data/

# Ignore large output files
outputs/*.pdf
outputs/*.html

Save the file.
Watch git react. Look at the Source Control tab — the files in raw_data/ and processed_data/ disappear from the list. Git is now ignoring them.
Commit the updated .gitignore. Stage it and commit with the message Extend .gitignore to exclude data files.







ImportantKey Takeaway



Keep your repository lean by tracking code, not data. Note where your data actually lives in your README instead.

section: 3. Publishing to GitHub with GitHub Desktop
text:
3. Publishing to GitHub with GitHub Desktop
Your project now has a local history. Let’s give it an online home so it’s backed up and shareable. We’ll use GitHub Desktop, which handles authentication through your browser — no SSH keys, no tokens.






NotePrerequisites




A free GitHub account
GitHub Desktop installed and signed in




Step 1: Sign In to GitHub Desktop

Open GitHub Desktop.
Go to File → Options → Accounts (macOS: GitHub Desktop → Settings → Accounts).
Click Sign in next to GitHub.com. Your browser opens — approve the request, and you’re authenticated.

That’s the entire authentication step. GitHub Desktop uses HTTPS behind the scenes, so there’s nothing else to configure.


Step 2: Add Your Existing Project

In GitHub Desktop, go to File → Add Local Repository.
Navigate to your project folder and select it.
Click Add Repository.

GitHub Desktop now shows your project and its full commit history — the same commits you made in Positron.


Step 3: Publish

Click the Publish repository button at the top.
Confirm the name and add a short description if you like.
Keep this code private — leave this checked for research work (uncheck it only if you intend the project to be public).
Click Publish repository.

GitHub Desktop uploads your project and its history to GitHub.com.






TipPositron ↔︎ GitHub Desktop



You can keep editing and committing in Positron, then switch to GitHub Desktop and click Push origin to send your latest commits to GitHub. Push whenever you want your online copy up to date.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
4. Seeing It on GitHub.com

Go to github.com and open Your repositories.
Click the repository you just published.

You should see all your files, and — by clicking the commits link (or the clock/history icon) — the complete history you built in Positron. Your local project now has an online backup.

Local-First vs. Remote-First
There are two ways a project’s life can begin:

Local-first (what we just did): you start on your own computer, build a history, then publish to GitHub. Like writing a document on your desktop and later uploading it to share.
Remote-first (cloning): the project already exists on GitHub. You clone it — downloading a complete copy, history and all, to your computer — before you start working. Like a colleague sharing a document that you download to edit.







Note



You’ll use the remote-first / clone workflow when you collaborate on someone else’s repository — see Appendix A.









NoteCan You…?




✓ Find the Source Control tab in Positron and read the U / M / A status indicators?
✓ Explain the modify → stage → commit workflow in your own words?
✓ Make a commit using the Positron Source Control panel?
✓ Explain why large data files shouldn’t be stored in git, and create a .gitignore to exclude them?
✓ Publish a local repository to GitHub using GitHub Desktop?
✓ Find your files and commit history on GitHub.com?
✓ Explain the difference between a local-first and a remote-first (clone) workflow?

section: Appendix A: Collaboration with Fork & Pull Requests
text:
Appendix A: Collaboration with Fork & Pull Requests
One of the most powerful aspects of version control is collaboration. This appendix walks through a complete, real-world workflow where one person proposes a change to another person’s project.

Understanding the Roles

Project Owner — owns the original repository and decides what changes to accept
Contributor — wants to suggest improvements, fixes, or additions



The Fork-and-Pull-Request Workflow

Fork — Contributor makes their own complete copy of the project
Clone — They download their copy to work on locally
Branch — They create a separate branch for their contribution
Edit — They make changes and commit them
Push — They upload changes to their fork on GitHub
Pull Request — They formally ask the owner to review and merge



Part 1: The Contributor’s Workflow

Step 1: Fork the Repository

Navigate to the project owner’s repository on GitHub.com
Click the Fork button in the top-right corner
GitHub creates a copy of the entire project under your own account







NoteWhat Forking Actually Does



Forking creates an exact copy of the entire project history — all commits, branches, and files — under your account. You can experiment freely without affecting the original project.




Step 2: Clone Your Fork to GitHub Desktop

In your forked repository, click the green <> Code button
Copy the HTTPS URL
Open GitHub Desktop → File → Clone Repository
Paste the URL, choose a save location, and click Clone



Step 3: Create a New Branch

In GitHub Desktop, click the Current Branch dropdown
Click New Branch
Give it a descriptive name (e.g., add-readme-documentation)
Click Create Branch
Click Publish branch







TipBranch Naming Conventions



Good branch names are descriptive, verb-focused, and lowercase with hyphens:

✓ add-ggplot-visualization
✓ fix-data-loading
✗ new-feature
✗ MyBranch





Step 4: Make Your Edits in Positron

In GitHub Desktop, click Open in Positron (or open the .Rproj file directly)
Create a new Markdown file: File → New File → Markdown File
Save it as README.md in the project root folder
Add the following content:

# Introduction to Programming in R: A Workshop Series 💻

Welcome! This repository was created as part of the 3-part
"Introduction to Programming in R" workshop series, part of the
**Advancing Reproducibility with Computational Skills (ARCS)**
initiative at the Yale Medical Library.

---

## Part 1: Fundamentals and Project Management

### In this workshop, you will learn to:
- Navigate the Positron interface and execute basic R commands
- Apply fundamental programming concepts (objects, functions,
  basic operations)
- Create vectors, data frames, and matrices
- Find a dataset in a public repository and read it into Positron
- Implement file organization and naming conventions for
  reproducible research

### Prerequisites:
- A computer with permissions to install software
- [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) and
  [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/) installation

---

## Part 2: Data Structures and Reports

### In this workshop, you will learn to:
- Manipulate vectors, lists, matrices, and data frames
- Implement literate programming principles in data analysis
- Generate dynamic reports using Quarto for reproducible
  documentation

### Prerequisites:
- Completion of Part 1
- [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) installation

---

## Part 3: Tidyverse Packages and Git

### In this workshop, you will learn to:
- Execute complex data transformations using `dplyr` and related
  packages
- Initialize git repositories and commit project changes
- Collaborate effectively using GitHub for version control

### Prerequisites:
- Completion of Part 2
- [GitHub Account](https://github.com/signup)
- [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com/)
- Windows users only: [Git Bash](https://git-scm.com/downloads/)






NoteWhy Add a README?



A README is the first thing people see when they visit a repository. It should explain what the project is about, how to get started, what prerequisites are needed, and how the project is organized. Good documentation makes your research more accessible and reproducible.




Step 5: Commit and Push

Switch back to GitHub Desktop
Review your changes by clicking the file names in the left panel
Write a commit message: Add README documentation for workshop series
Click Commit to [your-branch-name]
Click Push origin



Step 6: Open a Pull Request

After pushing, click Create Pull Request in GitHub Desktop
Give your PR a clear, descriptive title
In the description, explain what you changed and why
Click Create pull request

Example PR description:
## Summary
Added comprehensive README documentation to help users understand
the ARCS workshop series structure, objectives, and prerequisites.

## Changes Made
- Created README.md in the project root
- Documented all three workshop parts with learning objectives
- Listed prerequisites and installation links
- Updated RStudio references to Positron throughout

## Why This Improvement
The repository lacked documentation explaining what the series
covers, how the three parts build on each other, and what software
participants need.



Part 2: The Project Owner’s Review Process

Step 7: Review and Manage the Pull Request

Navigate to your original repository on GitHub.com
Click the Pull requests tab
Click the specific PR to review it
In Files changed, review the exact differences:

Green lines = additions
Red lines = deletions
Leave line-by-line comments for discussion

In Conversation, ask questions, request changes, or approve

Review options:

Approve and Merge: Click Merge pull request → Confirm merge
Request Changes: Leave comments asking for modifications first
Close without Merging: If the contribution doesn’t fit the project’s direction







ImportantCode Review Best Practices




Be constructive: Focus on the code, not the person
Be specific: Point to exact lines and suggest improvements
Be appreciative: Thank contributors for their time and effort
Test locally: For important changes, pull the branch and test it yourself before merging





After Merging
For the Project Owner:

The contribution is now part of the main project
The contributor’s branch can be safely deleted

For the Contributor:

Switch back to main and pull the latest changes
Delete your feature branch — it’s no longer needed
Your contribution is now part of the official project history!




Key Benefits of This Workflow

Safety: The original project is never at risk during development
Review: All changes go through a review process before integration
Discussion: Contributors and maintainers can discuss improvements openly
History: Every contribution is documented with clear attribution
Learning: Contributors improve their skills through feedback

section: Appendix B: Git on the Command Line
text:
Appendix B: Git on the Command Line
The Positron Source Control panel is a visual interface that runs git commands for you in the background. Here’s how to run those same commands yourself — useful for speed, advanced operations, and working on remote servers where no GUI is available.

The Basic Workflow

Open the Terminal in Positron (bottom panel).
Check the project status:

git status

Stage changes:

git add .
The . means “add all changed files in the current directory and subdirectories.” To stage a single file, name it: git add scripts/analysis.R.






NoteAbout Line Ending Warnings



On Windows you may see “CRLF will be replaced by LF the next time Git touches it.” This is normal — git is converting Windows-style line endings to Unix-style for consistency. You can safely ignore it.



Commit staged changes:

git commit -m "Describe what changed"

View the history:

git log --oneline


Verify What’s Being Ignored
After adding a .gitignore, confirm your data files are excluded:
git status --ignored
You should see your data folders listed under “Ignored files”.


Pushing to a Remote (CLI)
If you set up SSH (see Appendix C) or an HTTPS credential, you can connect and push from the terminal instead of GitHub Desktop:
git remote add origin git@github.com:username/yourreponame.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main






NoteGUI vs. CLI — When to Use Each










Approach
Best For




GUI (Source Control panel / GitHub Desktop)
Visual learners, reviewing diffs, getting started


CLI (Terminal)
Speed, advanced operations, remote servers



Many experienced users mix both: GUI for reviewing diffs, CLI for quick commits.

title: Git & Version Control
text:
Appendix C: SSH Key Authentication (Advanced)
GitHub Desktop handles authentication for you, so you don’t need this for the core workflow. But if you prefer to push from the command line, SSH keys let you authenticate securely without typing a password every time.






NoteSSH vs. Personal Access Tokens (PATs)



PATs are an alternative that use HTTPS, but they expire every 90 days and need renewal. SSH is preferred for long-term research projects because it’s a one-time setup. If SSH is blocked by your network, GitHub Desktop (HTTPS) is the reliable fallback.



Check for Existing SSH Keys
In the Positron Terminal, run:
ls ~/.ssh
If you see id_ed25519 or id_rsa, you already have keys — skip to Add Your Key to GitHub. Otherwise, continue.


Generate a New SSH Key

macOS / LinuxWindows



Generate the key (use your GitHub email):

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

Save the key. Press Enter to accept the default location.
Set a passphrase (optional). Press Enter twice to skip.
Start the SSH agent:

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

Add your key:

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Copy your public key:

pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub








NoteWindows Users: Use the Positron Terminal



These commands work in the Positron Terminal or Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows). We recommend the Positron Terminal for consistency.



Generate the key (use your GitHub email):

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"

Save the key. Press Enter to accept the default location.
Set a passphrase (optional). Press Enter twice to skip.
Start the SSH agent:

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

Add your key:

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa

Copy your public key:

cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | clip
If clip doesn’t work, run cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub and copy the output manually.






WarningWindows Troubleshooting



If ssh-agent won’t start, try running Positron or Git Bash as Administrator. If you see “Could not open a connection to your authentication agent,” run ssh-agent bash first, then retry ssh-add.











ImportantKeep Your Keys Safe!




The .pub file is your public key — safe to share with GitHub
The file without .pub is your private key — never share this
If someone asks for your SSH key, they always mean the public one





Add Your SSH Key to GitHub

Go to github.com and log in
Click your profile photo → Settings
In the left sidebar, click SSH and GPG keys
Click New SSH key
Add a descriptive title like My Positron Laptop
Paste your key in the Key field
Click Add SSH key



Test Your Connection
ssh -T git@github.com
Type yes if prompted about authenticity. You should see: Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...

title: Project Management
text:
Why Project Management?
Good project management is not just about staying organized — it is a core part of reproducible research. When you structure your project consistently from the start, you make it easier for collaborators, reviewers, and your future self to understand, rerun, and build on your work.
In this workshop series, we embed reproducibility skills directly into foundational coding instruction. This section introduces two practices you will use in every project going forward: initializing a reproducible R environment and writing documentation.

Creating an R Environment
We use renv to manage package versions in your project. This ensures that anyone who clones your repository can restore the exact same R environment you used — no more “it works on my machine” problems.

Navigate to the Console tab (left side of the panel)
Enter getwd() to check that you are in the directory you cloned. If not, navigate there before continuing.

getwd()

Once you are in the correct directory, enter

renv::init()






NoteWhat renv::init() does




Creates an renv/ folder

Creates or updates .gitignore to exclude the renv package cache
Snapshots any packages already detected in the project




Restart r







TipIn the console



You can do this with the circular arrow icon in the upper right of the console window.



To capture your current environment, enter:

renv::snapshot()
This records the package versions currently in use.






TipIn the console



If you get a message that says you are “in a project that hasn’t been activated yet”, choose option 1: Activate the project and use the project library



Take a look at your project directory in the Explorer pane in Positron. In your project directory, you will see new files created by renv:

├── .Rprofile
├── renv.lock
└── renv/

    └── activate.R
    └── settings.json
    └── library/
Now when this repository is cloned by a collaborator or reviewer, renv::restore() can find the renv files you have created and automatically load the matching package versions.

Scripts for Project Management
The following scripts are used in this workshop series. They are designed to be run in your local Positron session — copy them into your scripts/ folder and run them from there.






Important



Before Running These Scripts
These scripts load data files from your local raw_data/ folder. Make sure you have completed Exercises 1 and 2 and that your folder structure is in place before running them.



Metadata Cleaning for Analysis
This script creates the metadata file needed for further analysis, using the same dataset contrasted with Excel earlier in this workshop.
# Metadata Cleaning for Analysis
# This script creates the metadata file that we need for further analysis
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)

# Load data
metadata <- read.csv("raw_data/GSE113754_filtered_metadata.csv",
                     header = TRUE,
                     stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

# Create the desired output format
metadata_parsed <- metadata %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Clean up genotype column - convert "Shank3 Mutant" to "Shank3"
    genotype = case_when(
      str_detect(genotype, "WT") ~ "WT",
      str_detect(genotype, "Shank3") ~ "Shank3",
      TRUE ~ as.character(genotype)
    ),

    # Extract condition from characteristics column,
    # format and store in a new column called "Condition"
    Condition = case_when(
      str_detect(characteristics, "homecage control") ~ "_normal",
      str_detect(characteristics, "sleep deprivation") ~ "_sleep_deprived",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    ),

    # Create Geno_Cond column by combining results from the
    # "genotype" and "Condition" column mutations
    Geno_Cond = paste(genotype, str_remove(Condition, "^_"), sep = "_")
  ) %>%
  # Select only the columns you want in the final output
  dplyr::select(Sample = 1, genotype, Condition, Geno_Cond)

# Check the result
head(metadata_parsed)

# Save to CSV
write.csv(metadata_parsed, "Shank3_metadata_parsed.csv", row.names = FALSE)


Automate File Naming
This script demonstrates how to automatically add a timestamp to any R function and store the result in your outputs/ folder as a new file each time you call it. This ensures you never accidentally overwrite a previous result.
# Automate File Naming
# Automatically timestamps output files and stores them in the outputs/ folder

library(readxl)
library(writexl)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# Configuration section — update these paths for your project
CONFIG <- list(
  input_file = "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.xlsx",
  output_folder = "outputs",
  prefix = "LD_ProjectARCS"
)

# Function to generate timestamped filename
generate_filename <- function(prefix, analysis_type = "", extension = ".xlsx") {
  timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%dT%H%M%S")  # ISO 8601 format
  if (analysis_type != "") {
    filename <- paste0(timestamp, "_", prefix, "_", analysis_type, extension)
  } else {
    filename <- paste0(timestamp, "_", prefix, extension)
  }
  return(filename)
}

# Function to ensure output directory exists
ensure_output_dir <- function(output_folder) {
  if (!dir.exists(output_folder)) {
    dir.create(output_folder, recursive = TRUE)
    cat("Created output directory:", output_folder, "\n")
  }
}

# Function to load Excel data
load_excel_data <- function(file_path, sheet = 1) {
  cat("Loading data from:", file_path, "\n")
  data <- read_excel(file_path, sheet = sheet)
  cat("Data loaded successfully. Dimensions:", dim(data), "\n")
  return(data)
}

# Function to save results
save_results <- function(data, output_folder, prefix, analysis_type = "") {
  ensure_output_dir(output_folder)
  filename <- generate_filename(prefix, analysis_type)
  full_path <- file.path(output_folder, filename)
  write_xlsx(data, full_path)
  cat("Results saved to:", full_path, "\n")
  return(full_path)
}

# Analysis 1: Basic summary statistics
analysis_summary_stats <- function(df, output_folder, prefix) {
  cat("\n=== Running Summary Statistics Analysis ===\n")
  summary_data <- df %>%
    summarise_if(is.numeric, list(
      mean = ~mean(., na.rm = TRUE),
      median = ~median(., na.rm = TRUE),
      sd = ~sd(., na.rm = TRUE),
      min = ~min(., na.rm = TRUE),
      max = ~max(., na.rm = TRUE)
    ))
  save_path <- save_results(summary_data, output_folder, prefix, "summary_stats")
  return(summary_data)
}

# Analysis 2: Filtered data analysis
analysis_filtered_data <- function(df, output_folder, prefix,
                                   filter_condition = NULL) {
  cat("\n=== Running Filtered Data Analysis ===\n")
  if (!is.null(filter_condition)) {
    processed_data <- df %>%
      filter(eval(parse(text = filter_condition))) %>%
      arrange(desc(if(is.numeric(.[,1])) .[,1] else row_number()))
  } else {
    processed_data <- df %>%
      arrange(if(is.numeric(.[,1])) desc(.[,1]) else .[,1])
  }
  save_path <- save_results(processed_data, output_folder, prefix,
                            "filtered_data")
  return(processed_data)
}

# Analysis 3: Grouped analysis
analysis_grouped <- function(df, output_folder, prefix,
                             group_by_col = NULL) {
  cat("\n=== Running Grouped Analysis ===\n")
  if (!is.null(group_by_col) && group_by_col %in% names(df)) {
    grouped_data <- df %>%
      group_by(across(all_of(group_by_col))) %>%
      summarise_if(is.numeric, list(
        count = ~n(),
        mean = ~mean(., na.rm = TRUE),
        sum = ~sum(., na.rm = TRUE)
      ), .groups = 'drop')
  } else {
    first_char_col <- names(select_if(df, is.character))[1]
    if (!is.null(first_char_col)) {
      grouped_data <- df %>%
        count(across(all_of(first_char_col)), name = "frequency") %>%
        arrange(desc(frequency))
    } else {
      grouped_data <- data.frame(note = "No grouping column available")
    }
  }
  save_path <- save_results(grouped_data, output_folder, prefix,
                            "grouped_analysis")
  return(grouped_data)
}

# Main execution function
run_analysis <- function() {
  cat("=== Starting Analysis Pipeline ===\n")
  cat("Timestamp:", format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "\n\n")

  original_data <- load_excel_data(CONFIG$input_file)
  working_data <- original_data

  results <- list()
  results$summary <- analysis_summary_stats(
    working_data, CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix)
  results$filtered <- analysis_filtered_data(
    working_data, CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix)
  results$grouped <- analysis_grouped(
    working_data, CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix)

  cat("\n=== Analysis Pipeline Complete ===\n")
  cat("All results saved to:", CONFIG$output_folder, "\n")
  return(results)
}

# Helper function to run individual analyses
run_single_analysis <- function(analysis_type, ...) {
  original_data <- load_excel_data(CONFIG$input_file)
  working_data <- original_data
  switch(analysis_type,
    "summary"  = analysis_summary_stats(working_data,
                   CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix),
    "filtered" = analysis_filtered_data(working_data,
                   CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix, ...),
    "grouped"  = analysis_grouped(working_data,
                   CONFIG$output_folder, CONFIG$prefix, ...),
    stop("Unknown analysis type. Use 'summary', 'filtered', or 'grouped'")
  )
}

# To use this script:
# 1. Update the CONFIG section above with your file paths
# 2. Run all analyses:
results <- run_analysis()

# Or run individual analyses:
summary_result <- run_single_analysis("summary")
# filtered_result <- run_single_analysis("filtered",
#                      filter_condition = "column_name > 50")
grouped_result <- run_single_analysis("grouped",
                    group_by_col = "category")

What Are R Projects?

Self-contained workspace for each analysis or research project
Automatic working directory management. No more setwd()
Seamless integration with version control and documentation tools


Think of an R Project like having a dedicated laboratory bench for each experiment. Just like you wouldn’t mix chemicals from different experiments on the same bench, you shouldn’t mix files from different analyses in the same folder. When you open an R Project, R automatically “knows” where all your files are located - your data, scripts, outputs, and documentation all live together. This eliminates one of the most common beginner frustrations: the dreaded “Error: cannot open file” because R can’t find your data. The working directory is automatically set to your project folder, so file paths just work.

text:
WHEN and WHERE to Create R Projects

WHEN: At the very beginning, before writing any code
WHERE: Create a dedicated folder for each project inside of one “Code” or “R_Projects” folder
One R project = one research question/paper/analysis (not one project for all your R work)


The biggest mistake beginners make is creating one giant “R_Work” folder and throwing everything in there. Instead, think of each research question or manuscript as deserving its own project. Create the R Project FIRST, before you even download your data. This is like setting up your lab notebook before starting an experiment - it ensures everything stays organized from day one. Choose descriptive names that will make sense to you (and your collaborators) months later. A good rule of thumb: if you might publish this as a separate paper, it should be its own R Project. The folder location should be somewhere logical on your computer - many people create a “Research” or “Projects” folder in their Documents.

text:
Data Management Advantages to R Projects

Relative file paths work everywhere

input_file <- "raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.xlsx" #this
input_file <- "C:/Users/Username/Code/ARCS/raw_data/GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.xlsx" #NOT this

Share projects easily (zip the folder, send to collaborators/your future self)
Clear project boundaries (everything stays together)


Here’s where R Projects really shine for reproducibility. When you use relative paths like “data/metadata.csv”, your code works on any computer - yours, your advisor’s, your collaborator’s - as long as they have the project folder. No more changing file paths when you switch from your laptop to the lab computer! The automatic working directory means you’ll never again see that frustrated student debugging session where half the time is spent figuring out where R is looking for files. When you want to share your analysis, just zip the entire project folder - everything your collaborator needs is in one place. RStudio keeps track of your recent projects, so you can easily switch between your Shank3 analysis and your methods comparison without confusion. This organization becomes crucial when you’re juggling multiple research projects simultaneously.


.Rproj

Opening RStudio from an .Rproj file automatically sets the working directory to that folder
Lets RStudio remember project-specific session settings (like which files were open)
Your project appears in RStudio’s recent projects list
Everything just works - No need to hunt for files or set paths

The .Rproj File: Your Project’s “ID Card”
What it does: The .Rproj file is like an ID card that tells RStudio “this folder is a special R project folder.”
What happens when you double-click it: RStudio opens and automatically sets the working directory to that folder RStudio “remembers” project-specific settings (like which files were open) Your project appears in RStudio’s recent projects list Everything “just works” - no need to hunt for files or set paths

Version control system - like track changes for your entire project, not just one document

Remembers what changed

The .gitignore file is our first encounter with version control using git. Has anyone heard about this technology or used it before? What do you know about it? This is a technology that you will learn more about through the GitHub platform in part 3 of this class.
For now, you just need to know that git is a more powerful way of doing something like tracking changes and resolving differences if you and perhaps your collaborators iterate through different versions of a script and expand your project, or, if you need to roll back to an earlier version of your project, you can do that with Git. Git creates an audit-proof version of record for the coding work that you do. It can be one very important part of making your work reproducible.
Now, since Git pays attention to EVERY file in your project, we need to tell it which files to ignore - and that’s where .gitignore comes in…

text:
Building Reproducible Projects


What we just built:

Organized File Structure - dedicated folders
Protected Raw Data - original data stays untouched
R Project + Git - portable, trackable, self-contained
Complete README - project map, instructions, data sources




Why this matters:

Makes your project understandable
Anyone can run your analysis
Anyone can verify your results
Future-proofs your projects (when initialized early and modified regularly)



What we just did in this exercise is build the foundation of reproducible computational research. We created two things that work together: structure and documentation.
The file structure- separating raw data from processed data, organizing scripts and outputs - that’s not just about being neat. It creates a clear audit trail that anyone can follow. Your raw data folder is like evidence that stays untouched, while your folder structure shows exactly how data flows through your analysis.
The README we created is what makes your structured project actually usable. You could have the most organized folders in the world, but without documentation explaining what everything does and how to use it, it’s still a mystery to others - and to your future self.
Together, these create true computational reproducibility. Someone else can look at your project, quickly understand what you did, run your analysis, and get the same results. That’s the gold standard in research - work that others can independently verify.
Six months from now, when you’ve forgotten the details, this combination of clear organization and good documentation will be your lifeline. Ideally, you’ll open your project, read your README, and immediately know exactly what you were doing and how to continue.
This isn’t just good practice - it’s what separates amateur data analysis from trustworthy research, and what protects you as a researcher when funders, publishers, and peers ask you to show your work.

File Naming Conventions

No spaces (use underscore or en dash)
Start with dates using International Organization for Standardization (ISO)

YYYYMMDDHHMMSS

Use descriptive names


Let’s talk about something that seems simple but will save you hours of frustration: naming your files well.
First rule: no spaces in file names. Spaces are often special characters in programming languages that have a specific assigned use behind the scenes. Or, they may keep your computer from understanding that words belong together. Use underscores or dashes instead - both work fine, just pick one and stick with it.
For dates, I want you to learn the ISO standard: YYYY-MM-DD. So October 2, 2025 becomes 20251002. Why? Because when your computer sorts files alphabetically, they’ll automatically sort in chronological order too. The American date format won’t do this.
Be descriptive with your names. In six months when you’re looking through your files, ‘data.csv’ tells you nothing, but ‘participant_demographics.csv’ immediately tells you what’s inside.
The key is consistency. Whatever naming pattern you choose, use it for everything in your project. Your future self will thank you when you can find files instantly instead of opening each one to see what’s inside.”

text:
Convert README.txt to a Quarto Document

Navigate to your README.txt file in your ARCS project folder (PC: Windows Explorer; Mac: Finder)
Right click on the file and select Rename
Change the file extension from .txt to .qmd. You should see the icon next to the file name change.

if (!require("knitr")) install.packages("knitr")
if (!require("rmarkdown")) install.packages("rmarkdown")
if (!require("yaml")) install.packages("yaml")
if (!require("dplyr")) install.packages("dplyr")
if (!require("stringr")) install.packages("stringr")

Check if Quarto is installed in your environment by going to your terminal and entering

quarto --version
If you get a version number, that means it’s installed! If not, install from here: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/

Create a new file in your project root directory called _quarto.yml. Open it, then paste the lines below and save:

project:
  type: default
This gives Quarto a point of reference in your project.

Go to your README.qmd file and add triple backticks ( ``` ) before and after your README’s file structure tree to format it as a code block
In your terminal, enter

quarto render

In your terminal, enter

quarto preview readme.qmd
A browser window should open and display your README.qmd file as HTML






NoteWhat is localhost?



Notice that the browser window’s address starts with localhost followed by a port number. This means your computer is serving your .qmd file locally to itself — the file is not on the internet, it is being previewed from your own machine.

title: Reports
text:
Automate README.qmd Updates
Instead of manually updating your README every time your project structure changes, we can write an R code chunk that generates the file tree automatically each time you render.

Check whether you have the fs package installed:

library(fs)
If you get an error, install it first:
install.packages("fs")

Copy the script below:

#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| results: asis

library(fs)

# Get the actual structure
tree_output <- capture.output(dir_tree(".", recurse = 2))

# Define comments for specific files/folders
comments <- list(
  "raw_data"       = " (original data goes here)",
  "processed_data" = " (clean data goes here)",
  "scripts"        = " (code goes here)",
  "outputs"        = " (results and charts go here)",
  "README.qmd"     = " (project documentation)"
)

# Add comments to matching lines
for(item in seq_along(tree_output)) {
  line <- tree_output[item]
  for(name in names(comments)) {
    if(grepl(name, line)) {
      tree_output[item] <- paste0(line, comments[[name]])
      break
    }
  }
}

# Print the result
cat("```\n")
cat(paste(tree_output, collapse = "\n"))
cat("\n```\n")






NoteWhat this script does




dir_tree() generates a visual tree of your project folder up to 2 levels deep
capture.output() stores that tree as a character vector
The comments list defines annotations to add next to specific folders or files
The for loop finds matching lines and appends the annotations
cat() prints the result as a formatted code block in your rendered document




Paste this script into your README.qmd file in between the triple backticks where your file tree currently appears (it’s ok to paste over the directory tree)
Next to the opening triple backticks, add {r} to make it an R code chunk — it should look like this: ```{r}
Save your README.qmd file
In your terminal, enter quarto render then quarto preview readme.qmd
Go back to your browser window to see the result. Make any changes you would like to the comments <- list() section and re-render to see them reflected

text:
Create a Quarto Document for Publishing
In this exercise you will create a publication-quality document using a PLOS journal template, run a gene variability analysis, and generate a heatmap figure.

Setup

Check whether you have the following packages installed:

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
If any are missing, install them in your console:
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("readxl")
install.packages("scales")






TipChecking installed packages in Positron



You can also check in the Extensions pane by searching for the package name.




Install the PLOS Template

In your Terminal tab, run the following commands one at a time:

quarto add quarto-journals/plos
quarto use template quarto-journals/plos






NoteWhat this does



This installs a Quarto extension that formats your document to match PLOS journal submission requirements — including layout, fonts, and figure formatting. This is the same approach used for many other journal templates available through quarto-journals.




Gene Variability Analysis

Copy the code below and paste it into your publication.qmd file underneath the heading ## Gene Variability Analysis. Start your code block with ```{r} and close it with ```.







NoteAbout the #| lines



These are chunk options — they tell Quarto how to handle the output when this code runs inside a .qmd file. message: false suppresses package loading messages, and warning: false suppresses warnings.


#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Prepare data - rename the first column and use both ID columns
gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

# Calculate variance for each gene across all samples
gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression        = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance               = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Identify top 15 most variable genes
top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Display summary statistics
cat("Total genes analyzed:", nrow(gene_variability), "\n")
cat("Mean variance across all genes:",
    round(mean(gene_variability$variance, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("Most variable gene:", top_genes$gene_symbol[1],
    "with variance =", round(top_genes$variance[1], 2), "\n")

# Show the top 10 most variable genes
cat("\nTop 10 most variable genes:\n")
print(top_genes %>%
        select(gene_symbol, variance) %>%
        slice_head(n = 10) %>%
        mutate(variance = round(variance, 2)))


Data Visualization

Copy the code below and paste it into your publication.qmd file underneath the heading ## Data Visualization. Start your code block with ```{r} and close it with ```.

#| fig-cap: "Expression heatmap showing scaled expression levels of the
#|   15 most variable genes across all samples. Blue indicates
#|   below-average expression, white indicates average expression,
#|   and red indicates above-average expression for each gene."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

# Prepare heatmap data
heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

# Create heatmap visualization
expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low   = "blue",
    mid   = "white",
    high  = "red",
    name  = "Scaled\nExpression",
    limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob   = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x        = "Sample ID",
    y        = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x  = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y  = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    plot.title   = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid   = element_blank()
  )

print(expression_heatmap)

# Save high-resolution figure
ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
       plot   = expression_heatmap,
       width  = 10,
       height = 6,
       dpi    = 300)

Render your publication.qmd document to see your PLOS-formatted article







TipSaving your figure



Notice the ggsave() call at the end of the visualization block. This saves a high-resolution .png to your outputs/ folder with a timestamp in the filename — the same automated file naming pattern introduced in the Project Management section.

Cumbersome - it requires additional manual coding specifications based on the file type; it can be slow for large datasets; and can lead to unexpected behaviors with certain column types (i.e. converting character columns into factors)



readr package

Modern alternative to Base R and requires less configuration while being faster, cleaner, and provides less coding headaches (its does not convert character columns into factors) and uses the function read_csv, read_tsv, etc.
Returns a tibble, a modern data frame with features that make it print nicely, displays on a screen better, does not change variables names, and does not use row labels. The output when inspecting the data set using str() are nicer looking and more informative

haven package

The haven package is the dedicated tool for reading proprietary formats like SPSS (.sav), SAS (.xpt & .sas7bdat), and Stata (.dta), and is a key part of the Tidyverse ecosystem.

The openxlsx package is the dedicated tool for reading and writing data from Excel files (.xlsx) without needing external dependencies like Java. It is widely used for working with multi-sheet workbooks, applying styles, and handling complex Excel features, offering functions like read.xlsx() for import.
