Data cleaning and validation using the Tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of R packages designed around shared principles for efficient, readable data analysis. Install all packages at once with install.packages("tidyverse") and load with library(tidyverse).

Core Philosophy:

Tidy data structure: Each variable = column, each observation = row, each value = cell
Consistent syntax: Predictable function behavior across all packages
Human-centered design: Intuitive functions that reduce learning curve
Pipe workflows: Use %>% (|>) to chain operations for readable, step-by-step analysis



Key Benefits:

Uniform data structures using data frames/tibbles
Reproducible analysis with version control emphasis
Clean naming conventions (lowercase_with_underscores)
Active community support and best practices
Functional pipelines that transform data through logical steps

Note



apeglm is loaded here even though we never call it directly — lfcShrink() reaches it via type = "apeglm". Because that’s a string, renv cannot see the dependency when it scans your code, so without this library() call renv::snapshot() leaves apeglm out of the lockfile and Part 7 fails for anyone who restores from it. ✂️ Part 3 — Subset to a Simple Two-Group Comparison
Why subset? The full dataset contains samples from two conditions (normal and sleep-deprived) and two genotypes (WT and Shank3).
For this workshop we focus on a simple two-group comparison: Shank3 vs WT, using only the normal condition samples. This keeps the design formula simple and the results easier to interpret.

3.3 Drop unused factor levels after subsetting

info_sub$genotype <- droplevels(info_sub$genotype)



3.4 Set WT as the reference level (baseline for comparison)

🏗️ Part 4 — Build the DESeq2 Object

4.1 Create DESeqDataSet

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = counts_sub,   # genes x samples count matrix
  colData   = info_sub,     # sample metadata
  design    = ~ genotype    # simple two-group design
)







NoteUnderstanding the design formula



~ genotype tells DESeq2 to model gene expression as a function of genotype.
With WT set as the reference, all results will be expressed as Shank3 relative to WT.




4.2 Pre-filter Low-Count Genes
Keep genes with at least 10 counts in at least 3 samples (adjust thresholds based on your smallest group size).

keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3
dds  <- dds[keep, ]

cat("Genes remaining after filtering:", nrow(dds), "\n")

Genes remaining after filtering: 15742

title: Finding Differentially Expressed Genes with DESeq2
text:
🔬 Part 5 — Run DESeq2

dds <- DESeq(dds)







NoteWhat does DESeq() do?



Three steps happen automatically:

Size factor estimation — normalizes for differences in sequencing depth
Dispersion estimation — models count variability across samples
Model fitting — fits a negative binomial GLM and tests each gene

text:
📊 Part 6 — Quality Control

6.1 Transform Counts for Visualization
vst = Variance Stabilizing Transformation. It is faster than rlog() for larger datasets; both are suitable for QC.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)







Noteblind = TRUE vs blind = FALSE




blind = TRUE — the transformation ignores the design (used for QC and exploration)
blind = FALSE — the transformation uses the design (used for downstream visualization of results)





6.2 PCA Plot






TipWhat to look for in the PCA




Samples should cluster by genotype along PC1 (the axis of greatest variation)
Any outlier samples should be investigated before proceeding
If genotype is not the dominant source of variation, review your metadata




pca_data <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "genotype", returnData = TRUE)

pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar"))

pca_plot <- ggplot(pca_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = genotype, label = name)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("WT" = "#2196F3", "Shank3" = "#F44336")) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA: Shank3 vs WT (normal condition)",
    x = paste0("PC1: ", pct_var[1], "% variance"),
    y = paste0("PC2: ", pct_var[2], "% variance")
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

pca_plot




PCA of variance-stabilized counts, coloured by genotype.

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(path_figures, "PCA_Shank3vsWT.png"),

)

samp_dists <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))
samp_mat   <- as.matrix(samp_dists)

rownames(samp_mat) <- colnames(samp_mat) <-

# Display inline

TipWhy shrink fold changes?



Genes with low counts can have artificially extreme fold changes due to high variability. lfcShrink() pulls these estimates towards zero, making volcano plots and ranked gene lists more reliable.
Use res_shrunk for visualization. Use res for hypothesis testing.

section: The problem: “it works on my machine”
text:
The problem: “it works on my machine”

Your analysis runs perfectly… on your laptop
A collaborator runs the same code and it breaks
Different R version, different package version, different OS
Reproducible research can’t depend on whose computer it is

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
What is a container?
A single file that packages your entire computing environment:

the R installation
every package, at a pinned version
the system libraries underneath


Run that file anywhere → get exactly that environment.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
More than pinning packages

renv pins your R packages — good instinct, one layer up
But it still assumes R is installed, at a compatible version, on an OS with the right system libraries
A container ships all of it


renv is the shopping list. The container is the groceries.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
Not a virtual machine









Virtual machine
Container




Simulates
A whole computer + kernel
Nothing — shares the host kernel


Size
Gigabytes of overhead
Just your software


Start-up
Boots like a machine
Seconds, like a command




Containers borrow the Linux kernel — they don’t simulate one.
That’s why Apptainer needs Linux.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
Four words to keep straight







Term
What it is




Container
The idea: software packaged with all it needs


Image .sif
The file on disk — one shareable artifact


Apptainer
The program that builds and runs images


Definition .def
The text recipe for an image




Write a .def → Apptainer builds an image → Apptainer runs it.
Today: only the last step.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
So what is Apptainer?

Free, open-source software that builds and runs containers
A command-line program: exec, run, pull, build
Built at Lawrence Berkeley National Lab for shared clusters
Its answer to “hundreds of untrusted users”: the container runs as you


Formerly called Singularity — many clusters still use that command.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
Why Apptainer (not Docker)?

Built for research and HPC
Runs as you, not as root — works on shared clusters
One portable image file: analysis.sif
The image is the artifact you publish alongside your paper
Can still read Docker images — ours starts from one

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
The catch — and the lesson
Apptainer only runs on Linux
There is no Mac or Windows version.

title:
Introduction to
Programming in R Part 4:
Containerization with Apptainer
text:
…which is exactly the point
The host OS should not constrain what runs inside.
But you still need a Linux kernel somewhere:

On a Mac/Windows laptop → a Codespace (today)
On a cluster → the HPC login node
On a Linux laptop → it’s just there

title:

Host vs. container









Host
Container




What
Whatever’s installed locally
Fixed, pinned image


Controlled by
Each user
The definition file


Reproducible
By hand, fragile
Yes, by design


Use for
Exploration
Sharing / publishing / HPC
